HHV‐7 was detected in 78%, 47% and 52% of HIV‐seronegeative healthy blood donors (HD), HIV‐1‐seropositive long term nonprogressors (LTP) and progressors (P), respectively.
HHV‐7 and HHV‐6 are not stimulated by HIV infection.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the interaction between HHV‐6A and HHV‐7 with HIV‐1, in HIV‐1 seronegative healthy donors and in HIV‐1 infected patients.
the detection and characterization of HHV‐6 and HHV‐7 infections in HIV‐1 infected patients.
the opportunistic behavior and potential interactions of human roseoloviruses (HHV‐6 and HHV‐7) in patients infected with human immunodeficieny virus (HIV).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

HHV‐7 is not stimulated by HIV‐infection and does not interact with HIV‐1, but rather that HHV‐ 7 cell load reflects CD4+ lymphocyte count, with lower values in HIV‐infected patients than in healthy subjects, especially in long‐term HIV non‐progressors.
HHV‐7 does not appear to interact with HIV‐1 infection.
the HHV‐6 and HHV‐7 infections do not appear to be enhanced in HIV‐infected patients.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
HHV‐7 does not appear to interact with HIV‐1 in HIV patients.
human herpesvirus‐7 (HHV7) infection does not appear stimulated by HIV‐infection, but rather reflects CD4+ T cell count.

human herpesvirus (HHV)‐7 infection does reflect mainly the CD4+ cell number in patients infected with human immunodeficieny virus (HIV), with higher rates and cell loads in HIV‐seronegeative healthy donors and long term non‐progressors compared to HIV‐1‐progressors.
The main takeaway from our work is that
HHV‐7 is not stimulated by HIV‐infection.
HHV‐7 does not interact with HIV‐1, but rather reflects CD4+ T lymphocyte count.
HHV‐7 does not appear to play an opportunistic role in HIV‐1 infection.
